arxiv:2611.32884.text: Lazy Agents Answer Against Their Own Beliefs: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs Teaches Them to Act on What They Believe. From Richmond Sin Jing Xuan and colleagues. Long-task agents can guess too early, and rewards based only on the final answer cannot distinguish a lucky guess from an evidence-backed one. Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs uses the simulator's exact answer probabilities to reward agents for gathering more evidence when several answers remain, then committing when the evidence is sufficient. Across nine settings, it improves the base model by an average of seventeen point one percent, and beats a judge-based training method while using fewer computing hours. The trained agents also commit far less often when their own stated beliefs still allow several answers.

arxiv:2611.30634.text: Rewirable Circuits in Transformers with Loom Attention. From Da Xiao and colleagues. Transformers usually pass information through a fixed set of connections, which can limit how their internal circuits adapt. Loom attention lets each token dynamically connect attention heads, using one stream to control connections and another to store content. Across language modeling and downstream tasks, the resulting LoomFormer matches models trained with more than three times the compute and performs strongly against recent alternatives. With the same three hundred billion training tokens and only two percent extra computing, a two point eight billion parameter model matches or exceeds a twelve billion parameter model on tested tasks.

arxiv:2611.33010.text: Embodied AI Fails the Mirror Test: How a Simple Mirror Breaks Robot Policies. From Xuanchen Liu and colleagues. Robots often struggle to manipulate objects when reflections appear in their surroundings, but it is unclear whether mirrors themselves cause the problem. RoboDojo-Mirror tests five kinds of robot policies across ordinary scenes and several mirror setups, while comparing mirrors with solid panels of the same shape. Every mirror setup lowers success, with average drops ranging from ten point eight to fifty-six point seven percentage points across policies. Many failures happen without panel contact, pointing to confusion between real objects and their reflections.

arxiv:2611.32649.text: ICLWorld: Benchmarking In-Context Learning of Agents from Digital to Physical Worlds. From Qingle Liu and colleagues. Agents can now use both computers and robots, but it is hard to tell whether they can learn new rules while working. ICLWorld tests this across thirty digital and physical environments, using demonstrations in text or video and tasks that require applying custom rules. The strongest models succeeded on more than three quarters of computer tasks, but only about one quarter of robot tasks, and often knew a rule without acting on it. The results expose a gap between digital and physical abilities, and between understanding instructions and carrying them out.

arxiv:2611.32183.text: ThinkMorph-SSL: Scaling Interleaved Multimodal Reasoning with Pretext Tasks. From Jiawei Gu and colleagues. Interleaved multimodal reasoning lets models create images as intermediate steps, but training it often depends on hard-to-collect examples. ThinkMorph-SSL uses images themselves for supervision in a two-stage approach. First, models describe altered images, restore them, and interpret the results; then they learn from automatically built question-and-answer examples. At the same instruction-tuning budget, this approach beats instruction tuning alone and improves the base model by an average of eleven point three three accuracy points across twelve benchmarks.

arxiv:2611.31094.text: Unlocking the Power of Loops in Pretrained LLMs with Loop Residuals. From Xuanlei Zhao and colleagues. Turning a pretrained language model into a loop can add more computation without adding parameters, but earlier methods brought only small gains. LoopRes lets each repeated layer use outputs from earlier loops, while giving those outputs distinct identities and focusing attention on recent loops. Across six models and nine benchmarks, it delivers consistent gains; at twice the compute, it improves one model's performance by twenty-nine point one percent over standard fine-tuning. The gains extend to larger models, and performance scales better as computation grows.

arxiv:2611.27376.text: Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts: Toward Continual Post-Training. From Zhen Zhang and colleagues. As reinforcement-learning experts accumulate, combining them can require retraining and may weaken abilities outside their specialties. Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation keeps the original model frozen, teaches each expert through a small learned prompt, then combines prompts by stacking them without joint training. A single prompt recovers at least ninety percent of an expert's improvement in twenty-two of twenty-three settings, and the full combination matches multi-teacher distillation while generalizing best across six held-out benchmarks.

arxiv:2611.32554.text: PartAgent: Agentic 3D Part Segmentation via Expert Integration and Closed-Loop Refinement. From Yang Cao and colleagues. Breaking a three-dimensional object into meaningful parts requires both geometric understanding and semantic knowledge. PartAgent combines region proposals from a three-dimensional expert with part labels inferred by a two-dimensional expert from multiple views, then builds partitions at different levels of detail. It repeatedly checks its current segmentation and evidence, choosing targeted actions to repair or refine the result. PartAgent achieves the highest reported mean intersection-over-union across four datasets, outperforming competing methods by an average of 7.28 points.

arxiv:2611.30986.text: Reinforcing Diffusion Models by Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching. From Yihong Luo. Diffusion models can be aligned with rewards using reinforcement learning, but existing methods can become unstable when the model's behavior differs from the distribution used for training. Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching, or iTDM, addresses this by matching the model's instantaneous motion to the behavior distribution, with an auxiliary denoiser that removes unwanted baseline effects. Across image-generation and preference-alignment tasks, it achieves strong results in familiar and unseen settings. On a challenging benchmark, it converges nearly three times faster than competing methods and scales to a five-point-six-billion-parameter model.

arxiv:2611.32820.text: Residual Guidance for Real-Time Interactive Video Generation. From NaHyeon Park and colleagues. Real-time video generators can struggle to follow a new prompt, because earlier video content keeps steering what comes next. Residual Guidance measures this lingering influence without changing the model's stored context, then uses a correction during the early steps of generating the next video segment. Tests across single and repeated prompt changes show that it substantially improves prompt switching while largely preserving visual quality. It needs no training or model-specific tuning, and adds one processing pass per segment.

arxiv:2611.31974.text: Coding4Games: Can Modern Coding Agents Play Modern Video Games? From Shifang Zhao and colleagues. Modern video games demand that artificial intelligence handle complex visuals and make decisions over many actions, while systems that consult a language model during play can be costly and slow to respond. Coding4Games tests whether coding agents can instead build programs that play on their own, using visual input and standard controls. In tests across fifteen games, the best program beat the strongest computer-control baseline in thirteen and tied it in one, though human players beat all agents in ten. The benchmark also tracks how agents use feedback and improve their programs.

arxiv:2611.32067.text: LoopDVR: Looped Transformer for Efficient Dense Visual Recognition. From Sirui Liang and colleagues. Dense visual recognition models can use many parameters, making them costly to store. LoopDVR reduces that burden by reusing Transformer blocks in both the vision backbone and decoder, while adapters and careful weight sharing help preserve the distinct features learned at different depths. The framework also distills visual representations into the smaller backbone before task-specific training. Across dense recognition tasks, it achieves the best balance of accuracy and parameter count, cutting parameters by about twenty-eight percent while keeping accuracy competitive.

arxiv:2611.32617.text: VenusOCR2.0: Towards Efficient and Effective Document Parsing. From Lei Li and colleagues. Document parsing must read text, tables, and formulas accurately without becoming too slow. VenusOCR2.0 is a compact vision-language model, trained with a data process that uses its mistakes to guide expert checks and reliable supervision. On a document benchmark, it scored 96.45 overall and 98.57 on formula recognition, outperforming much larger general-purpose models. A parallel decoding module also made generation faster while producing exactly the same tokens as standard decoding.

arxiv:2611.31766.text: RoMo Hands: A Large Scale Richly Organized Text to Hand Motion Dataset. From Yizhak Ben-Shabat and colleagues. Generating realistic hand motion from text is held back by datasets that are small, coarsely described, or focused on rigid hands. RoMo Hands introduces about five hundred and forty-two thousand motion sequences, paired with captions that range from broad meanings to individual finger states. It also provides a new way to represent two-hand motion and benchmarks several types of generators. The tests reveal that matching a caption and producing physically plausible hand motion can pull in different directions.

arxiv:2611.32973.text: SpecEngineeringBench: Evaluating Coding Agents as Autonomous Specification Engineers. From Xingjian Wang and colleagues. Coding agents are expected not only to write tests, but to figure out what needs testing and where defects may be hiding. SpecEngineeringBench evaluates these skills using one hundred tasks drawn from open-source Python projects, with tasks for generating tests and finding defects through test results. Across seven leading agents, tests often passed and covered changed code, but detected relatively few defects, and pinpointing the exact function remained difficult. Generating new tests improved defect localization compared with relying on existing tests alone.

arxiv:2611.32736.text: Qwen-Image-HD: Autoregressive Diffusion for High Definition Image Generation. From Zihao Liu and colleagues. High-resolution image generators need long training sequences and heavy computation, and limited training can leave repetitive stripes in images. Qwen-Image-HD adapts an existing generator by training on local image tiles and producing them one at a time, using nearby high-resolution tiles and a small overview of the image so far. At four-kay resolution, it scores better overall than direct generation with FLUX-3-Image-Klein, and beats full-image fine-tuning of the same model in image quality while using less training compute and generating more efficiently. A parallel tile schedule also reduces the time needed to create a single image.

arxiv:2611.32462.text: MAGPIE: Agentic Multi-Reference Image Generation via Executable Scene Construction. From Yifan Dai and colleagues. Arranging several referenced subjects in the intended scene while preserving their appearance remains difficult. MAGPIE turns the instruction into a simple three-dimensional scene using an executable Blender program, then checks and revises the scene before image generation. A trained generator uses the rendered scene as a visual plan and the references for each subject's appearance. MAGPIE improves results with both Qwen and FLUX, including a twenty-eight point two one percentage-point gain for FLUX on DreamOmni2.

arxiv:2611.31466.text: AdProducer: Towards Agentic Advertising Video Generation. From Kunyang Li and colleagues. Turning a short advertising brief into a convincing video requires understanding the product and deciding how to show its value, not just generating images. AdProducer is an automated system that searches for product information and images, then builds a storyboard to guide a video generator. It is trained to improve both its storyboards and the resulting videos, and is tested on a new benchmark of advertising briefs. It raises product correctness and creative execution scores for two video generators, including one it was not trained on.

arxiv:2611.30235.text: PixelOne: From Options to Pixels in a Single Forward for GUI Grounding. From Kanghui Tian and colleagues. Precise screen clicks are hard to predict quickly, especially when shrinking a screenshot hides small controls. PixelOne teaches a model to search through screen regions, then transfers that spatial knowledge to a model that predicts a click directly from the full-resolution image. In one forward pass, it chooses a visual token and predicts the pixel within it. Across four benchmarks, its largest version reached 83.8 percent mean accuracy, the best among the tested single-pass systems, with an average latency of 0.43 seconds per target.

arxiv:2611.30597.text: ViDiHand2: Unifying Video Diffusion Priors and Hand Geometry for 3D Hand Motion Reconstruction in the Wild. From Yuxi Wang and colleagues. Recovering accurate three-dimensional hand motion from first-person video is difficult, especially when hands are hidden or cameras are unfamiliar. ViDiHand2 combines video diffusion predictions with hand geometry, estimating depth by matching image joints to a metric hand model and using observations across each clip. It also weighs geometric joint estimates against model predictions based on how confidently each joint is located. Across seven public datasets, it outperformed eighteen comparison methods, cutting joint error by forty-two percent and detection failures by about eight times versus the strongest baselines, while running at fifty-seven frames per second.

arxiv:2611.31126.text: WeaveVLA: 3D Relational Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Models. From Zien Wang and colleagues. Robot control models can follow language instructions, but their understanding of how objects relate in three-dimensional space, and how those relations change during a task, is often implicit. WeaveVLA makes those relations explicit, tracking spatial context across observations and using it to guide actions. It achieves over ninety-eight percent average success on LIBERO with two model backbones, and improves results on more challenging benchmark tests. In three real-world tasks, it also raises average success under both standard conditions and unfamiliar disturbances.

arxiv:2611.32968.text: Quantum-Inspired Tensor Train Spectral Solver for High-Resolution PDEs with Non-Periodic Boundary Conditions. From Sascha H. Hauck and colleagues. High-resolution spectral solvers work well for periodic problems, but non-periodic boundaries have been harder to handle efficiently with tensor trains. This work introduces fast cosine and sine transforms for Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions, using a shared tensor-train representation whose rank stays bounded as the grid grows. The measured ranks level off near thirty-two, even for grids with about sixty-seven million points. In tests, the method speeds up key solves and cuts memory use compared with existing tensor-train approaches, while maintaining comparable accuracy.

arxiv:2611.31752.text: Separating Measurement Failures from Defence Failures in Split Language-Model Privacy. From Georgios Politis and colleagues. Split language-model privacy tests can fail because attacks are poorly measured, but well-calibrated attacks can also expose real weaknesses. This review rechecks four prior test campaigns and two questions about what the tests cover, sorting each claim by whether it shows a breach, a non-detection, or something the evidence cannot settle. Only four of twenty-four required probes were qualified, yet they found privacy breaches in thirteen configurations; in a defence pilot, calibrated probes breached the privacy threshold in all seven tested cells. The findings also show that network protections do not hide activations from a compromised host, and weak information bounds cannot guarantee privacy.

arxiv:2611.33129.text: A Koashi, Imoto Criterion for Holevo-Rate Visible Compression. From Anthony M. Polloreno. Visible compression asks how efficiently a quantum source can be stored when the encoder knows each signal's classical label. This work gives an exact test for reaching the Holevo rate using shared classical randomness but no shared entanglement. In the source's Koashi–Imoto sectors, every signal must be pure on the quantum part of each sector it occupies; for qubits, the signals must all be pure or commute pairwise. Otherwise, codes with sufficiently small mean local error stay a fixed distance above the Holevo rate, regardless of blocklength.

arxiv:2611.31568.text: Heterogeneous Risk-Sensitive Evolutionary Learning in Coordination Games: Polarization, Welfare Loss, and Intervention for Efficiency. From Solaleh Mohammadi and colleagues. In coordination games, people with different attitudes to risk may settle on an outcome that wastes welfare. This study models two groups with fixed risk attitudes and examines their choices under best response learning with mutations. It identifies when the groups' long-run choices split between actions, even though that polarized outcome is worse than the payoff-dominant choice for both expected payoffs and risk-adjusted payoffs. Changing agents' risk attitudes can favor the payoff-dominant outcome, but both the share of agents changed and the strength of the change must be sufficient.

arxiv:2611.32930.text: Efficient inferential models and their fiducial connections. From Max Raner. Frequentist-valid inferential models can be built in many ways, and validity alone does not reveal which gives the most informative results. This work measures efficiency by the expected size of uncertainty regions and uses a weighted comparison to identify a generalized fiducial score as an efficiency benchmark. It then develops two ways to build valid models around that benchmark. Examples show that these repairs can improve on the benchmark by stepping outside the class of constructions in which it is optimal.

arxiv:2611.33068.text: The Reliability Function of Error-Correcting Output Codes with Noisy Binary Classifiers. From Gendo Kumoi and colleagues. Error-correcting output codes combine binary classifiers, but noise in their probability estimates can make their multi-class predictions less reliable than the Bayes classifier. This work models that noise as Gaussian and derives upper and lower bounds on the added error. The bounds show that greater separation between code words can reduce the excess error, while bounded separation between the most probable categories prevents it from disappearing. Tests on synthetic data and image-classification features support the predictions, and the analysis identifies cases where shared noise limits the benefit of any code.

arxiv:2611.32635.text: The sharp uniqueness threshold for the antiferromagnetic Potts model on regular trees. From Wei Wu and colleagues. Determining when an antiferromagnetic Potts model has a unique Gibbs state on a regular tree has been unresolved for some parameter choices. The work studies the model on rooted and regular trees, using a convex potential to analyze how the tree recursion changes color probabilities. It proves that uniqueness holds exactly when the edge weight meets a sharp threshold, with one stated exception. Combined with earlier work, the result also gives the exact critical power law when the threshold is positive.

arxiv:2611.32639.text: ReFocus: Progress-Guided Adaptive Practice for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation Reinforcement Learning. From Haoyuan Li and colleagues. Long-horizon robot tasks are hard to improve through reinforcement learning because success or failure gives little clue about where a policy gets stuck. ReFocus breaks tasks into stages, uses progress through those stages to find bottlenecks, then gives those task segments extra practice while continuing to update the full policy. On two simulation benchmarks, it achieves higher success rates than the baseline, reaching 97.8 percent and 51.3 percent. In a real-world bread-baking task, it reaches 95 percent success, compared with 30 percent for the baseline.

arxiv:2611.33148.text: CoT-Proxy: Cross-Format Transfer for Distilling Long-Horizon Policies. From Dawid J. Kopiczko and colleagues. Long-horizon agents are often trained by copying both a teacher's actions and its reasoning, but closed models keep that reasoning hidden. CoT-Proxy trains students using the teacher's actions alone, with the student's reasoning block left empty, and finds that the learned behavior transfers when the student is later allowed to think in its own style. Short summaries of the teacher's reasoning improve results further. On AppWorld, distilling a closed teacher raises one small model's success rate from seven percent to forty-eight percent, showing that hidden reasoning is not required for this approach.

arxiv:2611.32784.text: Convergence of Implicit Particle Methods for Wasserstein Gradient Flows. From Yunhong Deng and colleagues. Implicit particle methods approximate Wasserstein gradient flows, but nonlinear internal energy is difficult to compute from point particles. This work studies three ways to reconstruct the density: from particle spacings in one dimension, from smoothing kernels, and from transport maps. It proves that the resulting variational schemes and their minimizers converge to the continuum problem as the number of particles grows, with the time step fixed. The kernel method also converges as its smoothing is removed under a stated scaling condition.

arxiv:2611.32015.text: When Online Adaptation of Resilience Policies Hurts: Safe Exploration and Measurement Pitfalls in Resilience4j. From Rajat M. Barot and colleagues. Java microservices often keep resilience settings fixed, even though the best choice can change as a service's faults change. AdaptR4j lets a bandit learner switch circuit breaker, retry, and bulkhead settings at runtime using monitoring signals. Unchecked exploration performed worse than the default in three of four scenarios, but safer choices and bounded rewards helped it beat the default in every scenario where improvement was possible, and the best fixed setting when faults changed. A context-free learner did just as well, while a measurement error in an earlier test made severe failures look like excellent performance.

arxiv:2611.32769.text: Large-Scale Streaming Portfolio Optimization with Pauli Correlation Encoding. From Vicente P. Soloviev and colleagues. Large portfolios are hard to optimize because choosing assets from a vast universe creates a complex combinatorial problem. Pauli Correlation Encoding, which represents asset relationships using far fewer qubits than assets, is tested here in a rolling system that updates correlations and portfolios over time. Both it and a joint multi-cut variant consistently beat a Buy and Hold strategy, even during a downturn, when they lost less. The original method is more practical at large scale because the variant's resource needs and sensitivity to rebalancing frequency grow faster.

arxiv:2611.32960.text: From Safety-Driven Redundancy to Value-Driven Architecture: An ODD-Based Rationalization Framework for Level 4 Autonomous Vehicles. From Tiago Simão Ferreira and colleagues. Level four autonomous vehicles need backup systems to keep driving safely when key parts fail, but too much redundancy can raise design and maintenance costs. This study creates a framework that first rules out designs that do not meet safety needs for a vehicle's operating conditions, then compares feasible ways to reorganize or combine functions. In a simulated example, the best candidate cut modeled lifecycle cost by five point five five percent and stayed cost-reducing across all five thousand tested uncertainty cases. These are design candidates, not production-validated systems.

arxiv:2611.32414.text: Admissibility of Linear Time Series Models under Cone Constraints. From Won-Ki Seo. Additive linear time series models can conflict with constraints such as nonnegative densities or valid covariance matrices. This work gives a condition for when a stationary linear process stays inside a closed convex cone, and shows how the allowed randomness depends on the innovations and the filter. With unbounded lower tails, variation is limited to the cone's largest linear subspace; for quantiles, this permits only location shifts. The results also give ways to build nondegenerate models under constraints and show that certain partial sums stay bounded rather than growing like a random walk.

arxiv:2611.32886.text: The Capacity of Conference Key Agreement over GHZ Networks. From Hua Sun. The work asks how efficiently users can create a shared secret key from Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states held by different subsets of the group. It proves that the best rate is exactly the rate available from the classical data produced by measuring each state. Measuring first is optimal, even if users keep quantum memories and communicate publicly in many rounds. The same rate also describes how efficiently they can distill states shared by every user.

arxiv:2611.32322.text: Breaking Resonance: Square-root acceleration for Metropolis-adjusted randomized Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. From Nawaf Bou-Rabee. Fixed integration times can make Hamiltonian Monte Carlo resonate and mix poorly. Randomizing the integration time can break these resonances, and this work proves a mixing guarantee for the Metropolis-adjusted sampler with the velocity Verlet integrator, under a condition met by uniform, exponential, and triangular time choices. For strongly convex targets with a Lipschitz Hessian, the gradient cost scales with the square root of the condition number, alongside terms involving dimension and Hessian regularity. This is the first such square-root guarantee beyond Gaussian targets; without Hessian regularity, the cost can be much worse.

arxiv:2611.32918.text: InstructReplay: Replaying Assistant Turns to Preserve General Behavior During Factual Fine-Tuning. From Xiaofeng Shi and colleagues. Fine-tuning a language model with new facts can weaken its ability to follow instructions, reason, and write code. The damage often comes with shorter answers, and bigger changes in answer length go along with more failures. InstructReplay saves the model's answers to general instructions, then uses those answers during fine-tuning to help preserve its general behavior. Across three model families and two domains, it cut the average drop on five general benchmarks from twenty-eight point one to two point four, while learning new facts as well as standard fine-tuning.

arxiv:2611.33158.text: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments. From Xiang Fan and colleagues. Controlling many kinds of robots with one policy is difficult because robots differ in shape and movement, and those differences should change how they handle objects. OmniAct represents each robot's joints and connections alongside what it sees, then predicts movements suited to that robot. The team trained it using simulated tasks and trajectories for one million physically feasible robot designs. In held-out tests, it succeeded in sixty-three percent of episodes, and on an unseen real-world robot it achieved nearly twice the success rate of the next-best method.

arxiv:2611.31595.text: LUCID: Statistically Grounded Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning Evaluation. From Satiyabooshan Murugaboopathy and colleagues. Language-model raters can make systematic errors when judging reasoning steps, distorting audits and rankings. LUCID uses a small set of expert judgments to describe a rater's bias in plain language, then prompts it to regrade unseen steps, without retraining the model. On a math dataset, it reduced one rater's calibration gap from seven point eight to zero point nine percentage points, while cutting false alarms in half. The work also shows how statistical calibration can improve solution selection and estimates of sound reasoning.
